def: A posture kneeling with the chest lowered to the surface and hips raised. Used for rectal or pelvic examination and sometimes to reposition the fetus or relieve cord compression.
A nuclear imaging test using radiolabeled red blood cells to measure the heart's ejection fraction and wall motion. Also called a MUGA scan.
Death of brain tissue from loss of blood supply, i.e. an ischemic stroke. Causes neuronal coagulative then liquefactive necrosis over days.
Passage of gut bacteria across the intestinal wall into lymph nodes or the bloodstream. Can cause spontaneous bacterial peritonitis and sepsis, particularly in cirrhosis.
A surgical opening between the cecum and the abdominal wall for decompression or administering enemas.
A state in which the heart pumps more blood than normal, often with low vascular resistance. Causes include anemia, hyperthyroidism, AV fistula, beriberi and sepsis.
A surgical opening into the jejunum through the abdominal wall, used for feeding tubes when the stomach must be bypassed.
A surgical or endoscopic opening into the stomach through the abdominal wall, used for long-term feeding (PEG tube).
Clusters of nerve cell bodies that relay sympathetic signals from preganglionic to postganglionic neurons. Include the paravertebral chain and prevertebral ganglia (celiac, mesenteric).
Breast cancer surgery removing the whole breast and axillary lymph nodes while preserving the pectoralis major muscle.
Failure of the soft palate to close off the nasopharynx during speech, causing hypernasal speech and nasal regurgitation. Seen with cleft palate and 22q11 deletion.
A live attenuated vaccine against yellow fever virus. Contraindicated in immunocompromised people and in those with severe egg allergy.

A sudden, brief episode in an infant under 1 year with color change, breathing change or altered tone that resolves, with no explanation after evaluation. Replaced the term apparent life-threatening event.
A bruise of brain tissue from trauma, with blood leaking from small vessels. Often occurs at the frontal and temporal poles from impact against bony ridges.
Brain injury on the side opposite the site of impact, caused by the brain rebounding within the skull after sudden deceleration.
Narrowing of the left ventricular outflow tract below the aortic valve, from a fibrous ridge or hypertrophied septum. Causes a systolic ejection murmur and exertional symptoms.
Recurrent collapse or infection of the right middle lobe of the lung, caused by compression or obstruction of its bronchus by lymph nodes or tumor.
An eating disorder with limited food intake because of sensory aversion, fear of consequences or low interest, causing weight loss or deficiency, without body image distress.
A drug that binds a receptor and reduces its activity below baseline, producing an effect opposite to an agonist, unlike a neutral antagonist.
NREM parasomnias with incomplete waking from deep sleep, including sleepwalking, sleep terrors and confusional arousals. Common in children, with no memory of the event.
Talk therapy that explores unconscious conflicts and past relationships to resolve current emotional problems.
A time-limited therapy for depression that focuses on relationship problems, grief, role transitions and interpersonal conflict.
Legally ordered psychiatric hospitalization of a person who is dangerous to self or others, or gravely disabled, despite refusal.
The obligation of a clinician to warn a third party who is in serious danger from a patient, established by the Tarasoff case. An exception to confidentiality.
Periodic breathing in which breaths progressively deepen and then fade, with pauses of apnea between cycles. Seen in heart failure, stroke and at high altitude.
Resistance to instructions or doing the opposite of what is asked, without reason. A feature of catatonia.
Clumps of misfolded protein that accumulate in cells or tissue, such as amyloid, tau tangles and Lewy bodies in neurodegenerative disease.
A paraphilia of sexual arousal from inflicting physical or psychological suffering on another person.
A paraphilia of sexual arousal from being humiliated, beaten or made to suffer.
An NSAID prodrug that inhibits cyclooxygenase. Has less renal prostaglandin effect, and is used in familial adenomatous polyposis.
A G protein-coupled receptor (Gi) for somatostatin that inhibits hormone secretion. Targeted by octreotide; overexpressed in neuroendocrine tumors.

Bacterial meningitis caused by Neisseria meningitidis, with fever, neck stiffness and a petechial rash, spreading in crowded settings such as dormitories. Prophylaxis for contacts uses rifampin, ceftriaxone or ciprofloxacin.
A short-acting insulin secretagogue that closes pancreatic beta cell potassium channels, taken before meals for type 2 diabetes. Can cause hypoglycemia.
Planned vaginal delivery in a woman with a prior cesarean section. Main risk is uterine rupture.
An autosomal dominant disorder with a white forelock and patches of skin lacking melanocytes, due to KIT gene mutations.
A rare skin disease with orange-red scaly plaques, follicular keratotic papules and islands of unaffected skin, often with palmoplantar keratoderma.
Paradoxical closing of the vocal folds on inhalation, causing wheeze and stridor that mimics asthma.
A benign, self-limited skin condition of ring-shaped, flesh-colored papules, often on the hands and feet. Histology shows palisading granulomas around mucin; associated with diabetes.
Low arterial carbon dioxide. Caused by hyperventilation; leads to respiratory alkalosis, cerebral vasoconstriction and perioral tingling.
An asthma form whose only symptom is chronic dry cough, with no wheeze. Diagnosed by bronchial challenge or response to bronchodilators.
Surgical opening of the fallopian tube, used to remove an ectopic pregnancy while preserving the tube.
Surgical removal of a fallopian tube, used for tubal ectopic pregnancy or sterilization.
Sampling of fetal blood from the umbilical cord vein under ultrasound guidance. Used to diagnose fetal anemia and chromosomal or infectious conditions.
Delivery of a drug into the subarachnoid space around the spinal cord, putting it directly into cerebrospinal fluid.
Painless cervical dilation in the second trimester without contractions, leading to pregnancy loss or preterm birth. Treated with cerclage.
A confirmatory treponemal serologic test for syphilis that detects antibodies to Treponema pallidum by immunofluorescence.
Pain relief by injecting local anesthetic or opioid into the epidural space. Used in labor; complications include hypotension and post-dural puncture headache.
A sympathomimetic that releases norepinephrine and directly stimulates adrenergic receptors. Used to treat hypotension during anesthesia.
Inflammation of the fallopian tubes, usually from ascending infection (chlamydia, gonorrhea). Part of pelvic inflammatory disease and a cause of infertility and ectopic pregnancy.
Inflammation of the ovary, usually from spread of pelvic inflammatory disease. Autoimmune oophoritis causes premature ovarian failure.
Destruction of abnormal tissue by freezing it with a probe, used for tumors, arrhythmias and skin lesions.
Surgical removal of part or all of the vulva, used for vulvar cancer.
A G protein-coupled receptor on ovarian granulosa cells and testicular Sertoli cells that binds follicle-stimulating hormone and activates cAMP signaling.
A benign smooth muscle tumor, most often a uterine fibroid (leiomyoma).
A chronic daily headache from frequent use of analgesics, triptans or opioids, which then cause rebound pain as they wear off. Treated by withdrawal of the overused drug.
An ischemic stroke caused by a clot forming in a brain artery, usually on an atherosclerotic plaque. Contrasts with embolic stroke from a clot traveling from elsewhere.
Surgical removal of the thymus, used to treat thymoma and myasthenia gravis.

An older name for multiple system atrophy with prominent autonomic failure, causing orthostatic hypotension, urinary problems and parkinsonism. Alpha-synuclein glial cytoplasmic inclusions are characteristic.
A malformation of cortical development with disorganized layering of the cerebral cortex neurons. A common cause of drug-resistant epilepsy in children.
The satiety center of the hypothalamus. Lesions cause hyperphagia and obesity; stimulation suppresses hunger.
A fast heart rhythm arising from a single focus in the atria outside the sinus node, with abnormal P-wave morphology. Seen with digoxin toxicity.
Normal blood pressure in the clinic but elevated readings at home or on ambulatory monitoring. Carries increased cardiovascular risk.
A statin that inhibits HMG-CoA reductase to lower cholesterol, derived from the fungus Aspergillus. Side effects include myopathy and hepatotoxicity.
A sudden episode of anterograde amnesia lasting up to 24 hours with preserved personal identity and repetitive questioning, typically in middle-aged or older adults. Resolves completely.
Real-time x-ray imaging that shows moving structures, used to guide procedures and for barium studies.
Pain in the pelvic joints and surrounding ligaments, particularly the sacroiliac joints and pubic symphysis, common in pregnancy.

An autoimmune demyelinating neuropathy evolving over more than 8 weeks, causing symmetric weakness and sensory loss. Like Guillain-Barre but chronic, with albuminocytologic dissociation; responds to steroids and immunoglobulin.
Disease affecting multiple nerve roots and peripheral nerves together, as in Guillain-Barre syndrome.
Seizure-like episodes caused by psychological distress rather than abnormal brain electrical activity. EEG is normal during events; prolactin is not elevated.
Human chromosome carrying the VHL tumor suppressor gene at 3p25; its loss causes von Hippel-Lindau disease and clear cell renal carcinoma.
Weakness of the lateral rectus muscle from abducens (cranial nerve VI) injury, preventing outward eye movement and causing horizontal double vision with the eye turned inward.
A test of syncope in which the patient is tilted upright while heart rate and blood pressure are monitored, to provoke neurally mediated (vasovagal) fainting.
The shallow depression in the front of the skull floor, holding the frontal lobes and the cribriform plate. Fractures can cause CSF rhinorrhea and raccoon eyes.
An inherited disorder of muscle chloride channel (CLCN1), causing delayed muscle relaxation after contraction that improves with repeated use. Autosomal dominant (Thomsen) or recessive (Becker).
An autosomal dominant sodium channel disorder with episodes of muscle weakness triggered by rest after exercise or potassium intake, with high serum potassium.
Severe, disproportionate limb pain after injury, with swelling, skin color and temperature changes and allodynia. Previously called reflex sympathetic dystrophy.
Drugs such as clavulanic acid, sulbactam and tazobactam that block bacterial beta-lactamases, protecting penicillins from destruction.
A bacterial enzyme that hydrolyzes the beta-lactam ring of penicillins and cephalosporins, causing resistance.
Clubbing of the fingers with painful periosteal new bone formation along long bones, often secondary to lung cancer or chronic lung disease.
Low serum IgG, or deficiency of IgG subclasses, causing recurrent sinopulmonary infections with encapsulated bacteria.
A mass of undigested material, such as hair (trichobezoar) or plant fibers, trapped in the stomach or intestine, causing obstruction or ulceration.
Systematic error when an observer's expectations influence how outcomes are recorded or measured.
Fetal infection with rubella virus causing the triad of cataracts, deafness and cardiac defects (patent ductus arteriosus), plus blueberry muffin rash.
The peroxisomal transporter of very long chain fatty acids, mutated in X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy, leading to accumulation of these fatty acids.
A pump that lets a patient self-administer small, preset doses of pain medication, such as an opioid, by pressing a button.
Injection of hyaluronic acid into a joint, usually the knee, to improve lubrication in osteoarthritis.
A speech disorder with repetitions, prolongations and blocking of sounds that disrupt flow, i.e. stuttering. Starts in early childhood.
Pneumonia in infants caused by Chlamydia trachomatis acquired at birth, with staccato cough, tachypnea, eosinophilia and no fever. Treated with macrolides.
Twisting of the stomach on itself, causing obstruction. Classic Borchardt triad: severe epigastric pain, retching without vomiting and inability to pass a nasogastric tube.
A long-acting depot form of penicillin G injected intramuscularly, used for syphilis and rheumatic fever prophylaxis.
Eczematous, scaly nipple change caused by malignant cells (Paget cells) spreading from an underlying ductal carcinoma in situ.
Perception of sensation or pain in a limb that has been amputated, caused by cortical reorganization and nerve changes.
Both air and fluid in the pleural space, producing an air-fluid level on chest x-ray.
A benign skin cyst lined by stratified squamous epithelium that fills with keratin, forming a firm nodule with a central punctum.
Placement of a drainage tube into the gallbladder through the skin, used when cholecystectomy is too risky.
A benign, fluid-filled cyst usually at the right cardiophrenic angle, found incidentally on chest imaging.
Surgical replacement of the knee joint surfaces with prosthetic components, used for end-stage osteoarthritis.
Surgical reconstruction or replacement of a joint.
Narrowing of the urethra by scar, causing a weak stream and retention. Caused by trauma, infection (gonorrhea) or instrumentation.
Membrane channels that open when a neurotransmitter binds, allowing ions to flow and producing rapid synaptic responses. Examples are nicotinic acetylcholine, GABA-A and NMDA receptors.
Periodic self-insertion of a catheter to empty the bladder, used for neurogenic bladder and retention.
Equine antibody preparation that neutralizes circulating botulinum toxin. Used early in suspected botulism; does not reverse paralysis already present.
An aromatic solvent in glues and paint thinner, abused by inhalation. Causes renal tubular acidosis, hypokalemia and neurotoxicity; urine hippuric acid is raised.
Imaging of the aorta using contrast injected through a catheter, to evaluate aneurysm, dissection or branch vessels.
An uncircumcised foreskin retracted behind the glans that cannot be returned, constricting and swelling the glans. A urologic emergency.
Persistent difficulty or inability to ejaculate despite adequate stimulation. Can be caused by SSRIs or neurologic disease.
The removal of mucus and trapped particles from the airways by beating cilia. Impaired in cystic fibrosis, smoking and primary ciliary dyskinesia.
A positional headache, worse upright and relieved lying down, following lumbar puncture or epidural from leakage of cerebrospinal fluid.
Injection of the patient's own blood into the epidural space to seal a dural leak, treating post-dural puncture headache.
A carbonic anhydrase inhibitor like acetazolamide, used to lower eye pressure in glaucoma.
Obstruction of the common hepatic duct by a gallstone impacted in the cystic duct or neck of the gallbladder, causing jaundice.
A neutrophil protein; its level in stool is a marker of intestinal inflammation, used to separate inflammatory bowel disease from irritable bowel syndrome.
A diet limiting fermentable carbohydrates (oligosaccharides, disaccharides, monosaccharides and polyols) that can cause gas and diarrhea, used for irritable bowel syndrome.
Sweeteners such as sorbitol and xylitol that are poorly absorbed in the gut and can cause osmotic diarrhea.
The ligament on the inner side of the elbow that stabilizes against valgus stress. Injured in overhead throwers such as baseball pitchers.
Reconstruction of the elbow's ulnar collateral ligament using a tendon graft, common in baseball pitchers.
Effortless regurgitation of recently eaten food, which is re-chewed and swallowed or spit out, without nausea.
A receptor for endothelin that mediates vasodilation through nitric oxide in endothelium and clearance of endothelin. Also involved in enteric neuron migration (Hirschsprung disease).
A short repeated DNA sequence of a few hundred base pairs spread through the genome, such as Alu elements. Spread by retrotransposition.
Abnormal contact between the femoral head or neck and acetabulum, causing hip and groin pain with flexion and rotation.
An aneurysm caused by infection of the arterial wall, from septic emboli (as in endocarditis) or bacteremia.
A tear in the intima of the thoracic aorta allowing blood to split the vessel wall layers, causing tearing chest pain radiating to the back. Type A involves the ascending aorta and needs surgery.
Descent of the uterus into or through the vagina due to weak pelvic floor support, after childbirth or aging.
External monitoring of uterine contractions by a strain gauge on the maternal abdomen, usually with fetal heart rate tracing.
Lung inflammation 1 to 3 months after chest radiation, with cough, dyspnea and infiltrates conforming to the radiation field.
